title: FLMOP 14, 2026
author: Carousel: Teaching, Learning, Leading
summary: This piece diagnoses a common but under-named classroom problem: a 'looseness' in teacher instructions that lets low-level chatter escalate, not because students are badly behaved but because the teacher never specified how they should be participating while following an instruction. Drawing on Doug Lemov's concept of the 'means of participation,' the author shows that stating behavioral expectations after an instruction is too late, because students are already acting once they've heard the task. The proposed fix, Front Loading the Means of Participation (FLMOP), simply reverses the order — state the expected mode of behavior (silently, without calling out, etc.) before giving the instruction itself. The piece is careful to frame this as a nudge rather than a guarantee, and shows how it stacks with other instructional-clarity strategies like 'Anticipate Triggers.' It closes with the author's own testimony that this single, small script change was one of the most effective behavior-management levers they found early in their career.
points: Classroom 'looseness' isn't chaos and isn't defiance — it's usually the predictable result of never telling students how to behave while completing a task.
Once students hear an instruction they're already acting on it, so appending the behavioral expectation afterward ('...in silence') arrives too late to be absorbed.
FLMOP (Front Load the Means of Participation) simply reorders the script: state the expected mode of participation before the instruction, not after.
It's a nudge, not a guarantee — it works best combined with other techniques and can be repeated mid-instruction, not just at the very start.
quotes: If we want students to act in a certain way, we need to tell them what that is. Doug Lemov calls this the 'means of participation': quite literally the means by which students are participating at any given point.
Unfortunately, if the students heard the instruction, then they are already acting on it, and are unlikely to hear and properly assimilate the means of participation.
This is called Front Loading the Means of Participation, or FLMOP for short, and it's an extremely powerful way to create a classroom culture which is calm, quiet and efficient.

It's not guaranteed to work: FLMOP is a kind of behavioural nudge that gets students closer to doing the thing you want them to. Any teacher can do it, and in the majority of cases it will make a significant difference.

When I first started really learning how to manage behaviour, FLMOP was one of the first strategies I used, and in those early days made a huge difference to the overall calmness and productivity of my lessons.
